newsitem.title: ITALY: FOCUS - Italy unveils EMU law, plans debt conversion.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Italy unveils EMU law, plans debt conversion.

text.p: Italy, confident it will be a founder member of the European single currency, unveiled a draft law on Tuesday covering the introduction of the euro and said it would convert its debt mountain into the new money.
At a time when some analysts have raised doubts about the planned 1999 debut of the euro, Prime Minister Romano Prodi was eager to show that Italy for one would be ready.

"This is not just a formal thing but also a demonstration that we are going forward...it means we are beginning the operational aspects," Prodi told a news conference after his cabinet had approved the bill.

The draft law must be ratified by both houses of parliament, but there was expected to be little opposition to the package of largely technical proposals, with most Italian parties fervently in favour of European economic and monetary union (EMU).
Welcoming the bill, Treasury Minister Carlo Azeglio Ciampi announced that the government would convert all its negotiable public debt into euros from January 1, 1999.
"This will favour the creation of a critical mass in euros on the markets which will give assurances and will increase the credibility of the system," he said in a statement.
Belgium, France, Austria and Spain have already said they will convert their outstanding debt into the euro, while there is still some uncertainty over Germany's position.

Italy has more than 2,100 trillion lire ($1.2 trillion) of debt, the biggest amount of state debt in Europe, and the decision to convert virtually all of this into euro-denominated paper will add considerable weight to the new currency's debt market.
"It will immediately become competition for the dollar and yen markets without waiting for 2002," said Gregorio De Felice, head economist with Banca Commerciale Italiana in Milan.

The euro is due to be officially launched at the start of 1999, with the currency becoming mandatory for interbank transactions and the issue of new public debt for member states. Euro banknotes do not hit the streets until January 2002.
Treasury undersecretary and the chairman of the committee which drew up the euro bill, Roberto Pinza, said the law would cut the cost of the introduction of the currency to a minimum.

"We will avoid, where possible, the need for companies to keep double accounting...If a citizen or company chooses the euro, the public administration will talk to them in euros," Pinza said in a statement.

The centre-left government has staked its future on Italy qualifying for EMU at the outset and has pushed through nearly 100 trillion lire of deficit-cutting measures over the last year to clean up state accounts.

With both Germany and France seen struggling to tame their budget deficits to meet the terms of the Maastricht Treaty, some commentators have said a delay to the euro might be inevitable, but Ciampi warned against such talk.

"The government has realised from the outset that it is in the interests of our country to take part in creating a single currency and that any suggestion of a postponement is against the interests of Europe and of Italy," his statement said. $1 = 1,696 lire
